errors.english: what transgression would there be? It is stated that otherwise the fault is a grave offense.
errors.why: The quoted Vinaya passage is a question and answer: doing this, what offence is incurred? A sthūlātyaya. There is no 'otherwise', so the English wrongly suggests that restraining the emission is blameless.

fix.find: what transgression would there be? It is stated that otherwise the fault is a grave offense.
fix.replace: what offense is incurred? It is stated: a grave offense (sthūlātyaya).

errors.english: is to possess that [note: the offense]
errors.why: The commentary itself explains that 'possessing that' means possessing the effort/application (sbyor ba), i.e. 'not without effort', not 'the offense'.

errors.english: or who acts impulsively
errors.why: bab col du byung ba means that the emission happened accidentally or unintentionally, not that the monk acted impulsively.

note: A generally sound rendering of the saṃghāvaśeṣa 1 commentary, but the quoted ruling on restraint is misrendered as exculpatory.

errors.english: and arising from that [note: Tibetan: (de las byung ba); Sanskrit: (tadutpatti)] conforms to it
errors.why: It is the indicating capacity (gamakatva) that follows the determination of tādātmya/tadutpatti, not the determination that conforms to the capacity, as the next sentence ('if it did not conform to that determination') confirms.

errors.english: Previously, this commentary was set forth
errors.why: rnam 'grel here is the Vārttika (Pramāṇavārttika) verse being commented on, not 'this commentary'.

errors.english: it is because there is no unerring deviation (avyabhicāra) invariable concomitance
errors.why: The Tibetan says 'because there is non-deviation (avyabhicāra)'; 'no unerring deviation' is garbled and close to the opposite.

note: The argument about conjunction (saṃyoga) and the two relations is followed correctly, apart from some confused phrasing on the direction of dependence and on non-deviation.

errors.english: the very engagement of the cognition of an entity, by producing a discordant cause characterized as a latent impression, is cut off in its continuum by the cognition of the absence of the entity
errors.why: It is the cognition of absence that produces the discordant cause (a vāsanā) and thereby cuts off the continuum of the cognition of the entity; the English makes the entity-cognition the producer.

note: A careful rendering of a difficult passage on how conceptions of existence and non-existence are contradictory; the only slip is who produces the discordant vāsanā.
A faithful rendering of the discussion of when a karmavācanā counts as done, including the Upāli question on boundary-fixing.

errors.english: this relates to the object of perception
errors.why: dmigs pa is the verb 'is observed' (upalabhyate) of the root text, with which 'from which reason' is construed; it is not 'the object of perception'.

errors.english: Whichever word it depends upon, one must infer "from that cause."
errors.why: gang gi sgra is 'the word yad (which)': in dependence on it the correlative 'from that cause' is supplied; it is not 'whichever word'.

errors.english: The phrase "at that time" should be placed first, depending on whichever word is used
errors.why: The gloss says that, on this reading, 'that cause' (supplied from the word 'which') is placed first and construed with 'would be the nature of all'; 'at that time' is not the phrase to be moved.

errors.english: Even if any particular humor like wind were the cause, not every particular instance would possess all forms of desire and so forth. One must infer this by observing the certain result at all times.
errors.why: The whole gal te ... phyir ro clause is the anticipated objection introduced by 'But if the result...'; the English presents its first part as the author's own assertion.

errors.english: the objection is: "It is not so..."
errors.why: 'It is not so' is the root text's refutation of the doubt (the sentence ends 'dogs pa 'gog pa'o' on the next side), not the objection.

note: The humoral-causation argument is broadly recognisable, but the commentator's grammatical construals and the objection/reply boundaries are repeatedly misread.

errors.english: they are like those of a high-born person
errors.why: skyes here is 'a gift': when he meets the noble, his words become like a gift (they are welcome).

errors.english: He clearly demonstrates the meaning of the logical arguments.
errors.why: As the gloss on the next side shows, the verse means that with clear reasons he demonstrates the meanings, not that he demonstrates the meaning of the arguments.

note: The word-by-word commentary on the verses about eloquence is followed well; one lexical slip ('gift') and the misconstrued final verse.

errors.english: Who are victorious and adorned with the beauty of supreme things—
errors.why: 'Victorious' refers to the worshippers ('of those victorious ones, even the gods bear the garland of commands, variegated with the beauty of fine things'), and it is the garland, not the gods, that has the beauty.

note: The Tibetan verses are rendered faithfully (the parallel Sanskrit is left in notes), apart from the misattribution in the goddess's verse.

errors.english: Although the knowledge of the third mark [note: of the logical reason, which refers to the absence of the reason in the non-concordant class] is indeed established
errors.why: The phrase continues tshul from the previous side: tshul gsum pa'i rtags is the reason with three characteristics (trairūpya), not 'the third mark', and the note is wrong in consequence.

fix.find: Although the knowledge of the third mark [note: of the logical reason, which refers to the absence of the reason in the non-concordant class] is indeed established
fix.replace: Although the knowledge of the reason with three characteristics (trairūpya) is indeed established

errors.english: Alternatively, the negative concomitance where the reason is absent when the probandum is absent is not established merely by seeing
errors.why: The sentence says that neither anvaya (pervasion in all cases) nor vyatireka is established by merely seeing co-presence in some cases; the English splits it, so that the negation applies only to vyatireka and the 'or' reads as 'alternatively'.

errors.english: there must be a valid cognition [note: Tibetan: ཚད་མ་, Sanskrit: pramāṇa] that establishes the relation between the explained concordant class and the non-concordant class
errors.why: The point is that presence in sapakṣa and absence in vipakṣa, as described, are established only when there is a pramāṇa establishing the relation; it is not a relation 'between' the two classes.

note: The argument about why niścaya is mentioned is followed in outline, but the opening term is misread and the concomitance sentences are mis-segmented.

errors.english: "it is pervaded by one portion of the class of the subject of the sadhya [note: the thesis or that which is to be proven],"
errors.why: The statement is that the property of the subject (pakṣadharma) is pervaded by a portion of the pakṣa (i.e. the sādhyadharma); the English drops 'property' and garbles what is pervaded by what.

errors.english: Having explained the phrase "by a portion of that property of the subject,"
errors.why: These are the two words of the definition, 'pakṣadharma' and 'tadaṃśena' (by a portion of it, i.e. of the pakṣa), not 'a portion of that property of the subject'.

errors.english: since it is logical that the qualifier functions as the means of comprehension when the pervader is to be comprehended
errors.why: khyad/khyab par bya ba is the pervaded (vyāpya, the reason), not 'the qualifier': the pervaded makes the pervader known.

errors.english: positive and negative concomitance, which are to be pervaded, exist only within the qualifier itself
errors.why: The Tibetan says that the pervaded (vyāpya) has anvaya and vyatireka with respect to the pervader itself; 'which are to be pervaded' is misattached to the concomitances.

errors.english: is close at hand sentence continues on next page
errors.why: 'sentence continues on next page' is an editorial remark that has leaked into the translation unmarked.

note: The Hetubindu definition and the three possible restrictions are rendered with the pervader/pervaded/qualifier roles confused, so a specialist would need to rework the logic.

errors.english: If one kills someone thinking
errors.why: As the previous side shows, the patient is an animal belonging to someone (elephant, horse, camel, ox, donkey); killing 'someone' (a person) would be a different offence.

errors.english: If one hamstrings someone thinking
errors.why: The same: the hamstringing is of someone's animal, not of a person.

errors.english: and the carrier stationed on land within the border territory has no intent, there is no transgression. If the carrier stationed on land within the border territory does have intent, it is indeed a gross transgression.
errors.why: dgos pa med pa means 'does not require': there is no offence when the mantra/medicine transport needs no carrier standing on ground within the boundary, and a sthūlātyaya when there is such a carrier; intent is not mentioned.

fix.find: and the carrier stationed on land within the border territory has no intent, there is no transgression. If the carrier stationed on land within the border territory does have intent, it is indeed a gross transgression.
fix.replace: that does not require a carrier stationed on land within the border territory, there is no transgression. If there is a carrier stationed on land within the border territory, it is indeed a gross transgression.

note: The customs-evasion casuistry is mostly followed, but the victims of hamstringing and killing are turned into persons, and the final ruling hinges on an invented 'intent'.
